analysis.one_liner: Blocks the consumer bureau from restricting forced arbitration clauses in financial contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase a power Congress gave the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in 2010: the power to ban or limit contract clauses that force customers into private arbitration instead of court. If a bank, credit card issuer, or lender puts a mandatory arbitration clause in the fine print, a customer who is cheated generally cannot sue or join a class action and must take the dispute to a private arbitrator. This bill would permanently take away the government's ability to stop that practice.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card companies, lenders, debt collectors, and other financial firms that use mandatory arbitration clauses. They keep a dispute system where cases are heard one at a time by private arbitrators rather than in court, and where customers cannot band together in class actions that can produce large recoveries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, card issuers, and consumer lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the parts of Section 1028 of the Consumer Financial Protection Act that authorize the CFPB to prohibit or restrict pre-dispute arbitration agreements, leaving the bureau with only a study provision.
Without that authority, financial companies could continue requiring customers to sign away their right to sue in court as a condition of opening an account or taking a loan.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers. A person wronged by a bank or lender would have to pursue the claim alone in a private arbitration process, with no option to join others in a class action, and small individual losses would often go unclaimed entirely.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of arbitration argue it resolves disputes faster and more cheaply than court, and that class actions often deliver most of their value to class-action lawyers rather than customers.
The bill preserves the legal status quo as written in 2010, so industry groups would see it as protecting existing contract law rather than creating a new advantage.

Arbitration clauses typically allow the company to choose the arbitration provider, and arbitrators who rule against companies too often can be dropped from future rosters, a structural concern critics raise about the process itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a one-way transfer of legal power. It removes a government tool for limiting arbitration while leaving consumers with no replacement remedy — no court access, no class actions, and no agency rule to fall back on. The industry benefit (fewer and smaller legal claims) comes directly at the cost of the customers' ability to recover losses. If the bill had passed, that cost would have been locked in permanently.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick McHenry introduced the bill on May 22, 2014, after a subcommittee of the Financial Services Committee held hearings on the topic before the bill was introduced.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed.
Not a single other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms came out ahead without having to fight anything on the floor: the CFPB's power to restrict forced arbitration stayed unused, and existing arbitration clauses in bank and loan contracts remained in force. Consumers were spared nothing they were about to lose, but they also gained nothing, since the fine-print arbitration system kept operating as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms; the arbitration system stayed untouched

for.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the CFPB's authority to restrict mandatory pre-dispute arbitration.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Republican sponsored the bill, no one cosponsored it, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of support was never tested.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: These firms use mandatory arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court and out of class actions, which limits the total money customers can recover when companies are found to have cheated them. The bill would have guaranteed they keep that system permanently.

Firms dealing with financially stressed customers face frequent individual disputes; mandatory arbitration and a class-action ban shield them from the largest claims. The bill would protect that arrangement from agency rules.

Arbitration firms earn fees for hearing consumer financial disputes; a restriction on mandatory clauses would shrink that market. The bill keeps the market intact by blocking the regulator who could limit it.
